[A research synthesis drawing on policy documents, histories of education and critical analyses of textbooks. Full references at the end.]{.marginnote}*Christian National Education and Zionist state pedagogy*\
South Africa, 1948–1994 · Israel today\
[Comparative study · History of education · Textbook analysis]{.smallcaps}

# 1. Summary

This synthesis compares how two ethno-nationalist states used schooling to shape collective memory, entrench racial and territorial hierarchies, and prepare the young for military service.

In South Africa, Christian National Education (CNE) was an explicit Calvinist blueprint that presented segregation, mother-tongue separation and white supremacy as God's plan.[@Bloomberg1989; @Christie1986; @ICNO1948] Bantu Education added separate, unequal schooling to keep Black South Africans in subordinate labour.[@Christie1986; @Hofmeyr1982]

In Israel, according to Peled-Elhanan and others, textbook images, maps and omissions teach a "cult of continuity" and cast Palestinians as a demographic threat or an enemy.[@PeledElhanan2012; @Podeh2002; @Yiftachel2006] The methods are subtler than CNE's and sit alongside a democratic self-image.[@PeledElhanan2012; @Stanley2015]

::: {.verdict label="Main finding"}
Both systems used school to make group dominance look natural and to prepare the young to defend it.
:::

# 2. Scope

[Schools in divided societies]{.newthought} are rarely neutral. Critical sociologists of education argue that state schooling manages ideology, shapes national identity and reproduces state power.[@Ellul1965; @Illich1971; @Stanley2015] When an ethno-nationalist movement holds the state, the curriculum justifies the subjugation or removal of indigenous people and readies the dominant group's young for compliance and conscription.[@Bloomberg1989; @PeledElhanan2012]

The cases are CNE under the National Party (1948–1994) and the textbooks of state-funded Israeli schools, as documented by Nurit Peled-Elhanan and other critical historians. Both rely on sacred origin myths, on "re-indigenisation" (recasting the dominant group as the land's rightful natives), on dehumanising the out-group and on militarised civic education.[@Bloomberg1989; @Christie1986; @Hexham1981; @PeledElhanan2012]

The study reads South African policy, including the 1948 *Christelik-Nasionale Onderwysbeleid* and the National Education Policy Act of 1967, against analyses of Israeli textbooks.[@Christie1986; @ICNO1948; @PeledElhanan2012; @VanLeeuwen2008]

# 3. Founding myths

Indoctrination starts with a founding narrative, an ideological "hypotext", that makes the dominant group's power legitimate. Both states based education policy on myths of a chosen people with a divine or civilising mission.[@Bloomberg1989; @Hexham1981; @PeledElhanan2012]

[ICNO: *Instituut vir Christelik-Nasionale Onderwys*. FAK: *Federasie van Afrikaanse Kultuurvereniginge*.]{.marginnote}[In South Africa]{.newthought}, the ICNO codified CNE in 1948. The institute was an arm of the FAK, which the secret Afrikaner *Broederbond* controlled. Drawing on the Dutch neo-Calvinists Abraham Kuyper and Herman Bavinck, CNE held that God created separate nations, languages and races, each with a set destiny. Article 1 of the 1948 policy required Afrikaans-speaking children to be taught strictly in Calvinist scripture and fervent patriotism. History was taught as the unfolding of God's plan, with Afrikaner victories over indigenous Black people celebrated as divine protection of a Christian civilisation.[@Bloomberg1989; @Christie1986; @Hexham1981; @Hofmeyr1982; @ICNO1948]

In Israel, mainstream state education carries what Peled-Elhanan calls the "Grand Zionist Narrative": secularised biblical myth joined to modern ethno-nationalism to build a "cult of continuity". History, geography and civics textbooks present Jewish history as an unbroken 2,000-year struggle against persecution, ending in the "redemption of the land" and national rebirth in 1948. Shaping collective memory in the way Nora and Wertsch describe, they leave out 1,300 years of continuous Palestinian life and show Jewish immigrants as "re-indigenised" owners returning to an empty wilderness.[@PeledElhanan2012; @Podeh2002]

<!-- TODO: The source names Nora and Wertsch on collective memory but gives no citation or bibliography entry for either. -->

| Dimension                | Apartheid South Africa (CNE)                        | Israel (Zionist narrative)                          |
|--------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------|
| Founding story | Neo-Calvinist predestination; Afrikaner divine mission        | Secularised biblical myth; "cult of continuity"     |
| The out-group  | Europeans as "senior trustee"; separate racial compartments   | "Primitive" Arabs; terrorist and demographic threat |
| Methods        | Scripture across the curriculum; veld schools; Youth Preparedness | Images and layout; redrawn maps; omission       |
| Civic aim      | Readiness against the "total onslaught"; anti-communism       | Readiness for conscription; combat motivation       |

# 4. Textbooks and the out-group

Both regimes dehumanised or erased the subjugated group in approved learning materials, by different means.[@Christie1986; @PeledElhanan2012]

[In Israeli textbooks]{.newthought}, Peled-Elhanan shows how text, maps, photographs and layout combine to marginalise Palestinians:[@PeledElhanan2012; @VanLeeuwen2008]

- *Generic labels.* Palestinians seldom appear as individuals with names, families or work, but as "the Arabs", "the non-Jewish population" or "infiltrators".
- *Defined by threat.* When they do appear, it is through negative acts: lurking, throwing stones, attacking, refusing progress. The Israeli army appears civilised, lawful and heroic, even when carrying out punitive demolitions or massacres.
- *Expulsion recast.* The displacement of 800,000 Palestinians in the 1948 war, the *Nakba*, is described as "flight", "desertion" or "panic", which relieves the state of moral responsibility. The 2011 "Nakba Law" penalises educational bodies that commemorate it.[@PeledElhanan2012; @Podeh2002] <!-- TODO: Check the 800,000 figure (estimates commonly given are 700,000–750,000) and the description of the 2011 law, which as usually reported lets the state cut funding to state-funded bodies, not specifically educational ones. -->

In South Africa, CNE built the Black out-group through open racial hierarchy and paternalism. The 1948 policy said that Black ("native") education must rest on the European's worldview, and that "the Boer nation is the senior European trustee of the native". Under the Bantu Education Act of 1953, schooling for Black children was deliberately degraded to train them only for manual and domestic labour, in line with the state's aim that Black South Africans remain "hewers of wood and drawers of water".[@Bloomberg1989; @Christie1986; @Hofmeyr1982]

# 5. Schooling for war

Both systems conditioned young people to accept permanent militarisation and the defence of the state against existential threats.[@Christie1986; @PeledElhanan2012]

[In the 1970s and 1980s]{.newthought}, South Africa brought the Youth Preparedness Programme and compulsory veld schools into white secondary schools. Built around the military doctrine of a "total onslaught" by international communism and the liberation movements, Youth Preparedness combined moral re-armament, obstacle courses, bush survival and anti-communist teaching. Veld schools took city children into the countryside for lectures on patriotism, creationism and racial boundaries, to instil obedience and military readiness.[@Christie1986]

Israeli students face the draft at 18. Peled-Elhanan argues that history and geography textbooks prepare them for it: they are written for teenagers who will soon enforce the occupation and may use lethal force in the Palestinian territories. The books present military operations as moral necessity, Palestinian resistance as irrational hostility, and soldiers as selfless defenders of the homeland.[@PeledElhanan2012]

|                    | South Africa, 1970s–1980s                              | Israel, 1990s to the present                        |
|--------------------|--------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------|
| Threat    | "Total onslaught"; communism                                  | "Terrorism"; existential demographic threat         |
| Means     | Youth Preparedness and veld schools                           | History and civics textbooks; heroic images of the army |
| Goal      | White youth ready for conscription, border wars and township control | 18-year-olds ready for the draft and the occupation |

The study names three outcomes common to both: a sense of ethno-national supremacy under siege; no empathy for the subjugated indigenous population; and acceptance of segregation and of state violence outside the law. <!-- TODO: The source states these outcomes in a diagram without citing a source for them. -->

# 6. Where they differ

[Theology against secular nationalism.]{.newthought} CNE was openly confessional, using Calvinist doctrine and church authority to justify segregation.[@Bloomberg1989; @Hexham1981] Israeli state education makes its claims in the language of secular geography, civic democracy and archaeology, while still drawing on the biblical "Promised Land" to support territorial expansion. That lets Israel keep a "Jewish and democratic" self-image in line with Western liberal norms, though Yiftachel calls the system an "ethnocracy".[@PeledElhanan2012; @Yiftachel2006]

*Separation against absorption.* Apartheid South Africa split schooling into separate, unequal departments for Whites, Africans, Coloureds and Indians.[@Christie1986; @Malherbe1977] Israel has one Ministry of Education over Jewish (secular and religious) and Arab public schools. But Peled-Elhanan shows that Palestinian-Arab citizens in those schools follow a curriculum that censors their national history, denies the *Nakba* and imposes Zionist historiography. They are, in effect, shut out of their own history.[@PeledElhanan2012]

::: {.verdict label="The key difference"}
South Africa enforced dominance in the open, through church doctrine and separate schools. Israel does it inside one system that presents itself as secular and democratic.
:::

# 7. Limits of the sources

1. *Policy is not practice.* Studies of CNE policy and of textbook imagery tend to assume the message arrived intact. In classrooms it was contested: teachers resisted, students organised (the 1976 Soweto uprising among them), and communities built alternatives.[@Christie1986; @ICNO1948; @PeledElhanan2012]
2. *Textbooks change.* Peled-Elhanan records a shift in the 2000s towards simpler, right-wing narratives. But the late 1990s saw brief post-Zionist revisions, such as Eyal Naveh's textbooks, which point to disputes within the ministry.[@PeledElhanan2012; @Podeh2002]

# 8. Conclusion

Ethno-nationalist regimes use education to manufacture consent, build an exclusive collective memory and make inequality look natural. CNE did it with Calvinist theology and paramilitary training; Israeli textbooks do it with imagery, maps and omission. Taking state curricula apart is how these mechanisms come to light.
